name: The Legal Ground
title: The Legal Ground
answer: Schools still have legal duties to English learners even though the Department of Education rescinded its 2015 guidance letter in August 2025. The rescission changed guidance, not law: Title VI, Lau v. Nichols, the Castañeda v. Pickard standard, and Every Student Succeeds Act requirements remain in place. Schools must still give English learners meaningful access to grade level content.

sections.body: This idea concerns the legal ground under English learner education in the United States. Schools have long been required to help students overcome language barriers, through Title VI of the Civil Rights Act, the Supreme Court's decision in Lau v. Nichols, and the Castañeda v. Pickard standard. In 2015 the Departments of Education and Justice issued a detailed letter explaining how schools could meet those duties. In August 2025 the Department of Education rescinded that letter, saying it did not align with the administration's priorities. The problem this idea addresses is the confusion that follows when guidance is withdrawn, because educators may wrongly assume the underlying obligations have gone too.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In practice, schools continue to carry out the duties the rescinded letter described. The text does not set out separate steps by grade band, so the work applies across a school's English learner program rather than to one age group. Districts should watch their state education agency for guidance, since many states have their own laws on English learner education. They should also check the status of federal changes before relying on any federal resource. The federal office that oversees English learner programs is itself in flux, because in April 2026 the Department of Education notified Congress that it planned to dissolve its Office of English Language Acquisition.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text labels this material as legal and policy background rather than research evidence. It cites Education Week in 2025 for the rescission of the 2015 letter and for the point that the letter was not legally binding and that the statutes and court decisions it described remain in place. It cites Education Week in 2026 for the Department of Education's notification to Congress that it planned to dissolve its Office of English Language Acquisition. It cites Colorín Colorado in 2025 for the continuing Every Student Succeeds Act requirements and for state laws on English learner education. Advocates quoted in the text note that schools' federal duties to these students remain with or without the office.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text sets clear limits on what the rescission means. The change was to guidance, not to law, and the letter was never legally binding, so the statutes and court decisions it described still stand. Every Student Succeeds Act requirements for English learners still apply, and state laws add their own duties. The federal office that oversees these programs is in flux, and the text advises districts to watch their state education agency and to check the status of these changes before relying on any federal resource. Decisions about how to meet these duties stay with schools and districts, and nothing here is legal advice.
